items.summary: Fixes for those embedding Frida, with @kkuehl tracking down a crash when creating a second DeviceManager and a hang on deinit. Also in this one: @Cassian433 made thread enumeration work in a spawned process that hasn’t been resumed yet, and @hsorbo taught our XPC client about messages that want a reply. Embedders Kirby found that creating a DeviceManager after another one had attached to the system session and been closed crashed. This is a regression from 17.27.6, where the agent moved into a shared resource directory. Its image then outlived the session that had shut its GLib down, so loading it into our own process a second time ran its environment init against a type system that was already gone. There is now one agent container per process, created on first use and torn down by frida_shutdown() or frida_deinit() , and a host session only closes its own sessions in it. He also found that frida_deinit() hung whenever idund was running. Stopping Idun’s device monitor left its backends in place, and the daemon backend’s client kept a D-Bus connection alive, which kept GLib’s D-Bus worker alive, so shutting GIO down waited forever. Thanks, Kirby! Linux @Cassian433 fixed Process.enumerateThreads() returning an empty array in a process that was spawned and not yet resumed, which @JingMatrix reported last year. Reading a thread’s registers means attaching to it with ptrace() , which fails when another process is already tracing it, as our helper is with the main thread of a process it has paused. Such a thread is now kept, just without its CPU context. Thanks! On musl, the agent stays loaded across injections. Threads stopped during unload could report garbage after the agent’s runner was gone, leaving a flag set with nothing scheduled, which disabled thread garbage collection in every later session. iOS Håvard noticed that CoreDevice’s streaming actions, such as streamapplist , never delivered anything. They push their results as messages flagged as wanting a reply, which Idun’s XPC connection silently dropped unless they were replies themselves. Those are now forwarded, and our Fruity backend acknowledges each one, as devicectl does. Thanks! GLib A leak in our GLib is gone. If code on a new thread asks for the current thread before GLib’s own thread entrypoint runs, as an Interceptor hook on libc’s thread entrypoint may, GLib creates a placeholder and queues cleanups on it. The placeholder was then replaced without being destroyed, along with everything it was meant to clean up. Enjoy! Changelog agent-container: Share one container across host sessions, fixing a crash when creating a second DeviceManager . Thanks @kkuehl ! idun: Release the device monitor’s backends on stop, fixing frida_deinit() hanging while idund is running. Thanks @kkuehl ! linux: Keep threads whose registers can’t be read. Thanks @Cassian433 and @JingMatrix ! agent: Don’t wedge thread garbage collection on garbage reported during teardown. glib: Adopt the placeholder thread in the thread proxy, fixing a leak. idun: Forward XPC messages that want a reply. Thanks @hsorbo ! fruity: Acknowledge XPC messages that want a reply. Thanks @hsorbo !
items.summary_html:
Fixes for those embedding Frida, with @kkuehl tracking down a crash when creating a second DeviceManager and a hang on deinit. Also in this one: @Cassian433 made thread enumeration work in a spawned process that hasn’t been resumed yet, and @hsorbo taught our XPC client about messages that want a reply.

Embedders

Kirby found that creating a DeviceManager after another one had attached to the system session and been closed crashed. This is a regression from 17.27.6, where the agent moved into a shared resource directory. Its image then outlived the session that had shut its GLib down, so loading it into our own process a second time ran its environment init against a type system that was already gone. There is now one agent container per process, created on first use and torn down by frida_shutdown() or frida_deinit(), and a host session only closes its own sessions in it.

He also found that frida_deinit() hung whenever idund was running. Stopping Idun’s device monitor left its backends in place, and the daemon backend’s client kept a D-Bus connection alive, which kept GLib’s D-Bus worker alive, so shutting GIO down waited forever. Thanks, Kirby!

Linux

@Cassian433 fixed Process.enumerateThreads() returning an empty array in a process that was spawned and not yet resumed, which @JingMatrix reported last year. Reading a thread’s registers means attaching to it with ptrace(), which fails when another process is already tracing it, as our helper is with the main thread of a process it has paused. Such a thread is now kept, just without its CPU context. Thanks!

On musl, the agent stays loaded across injections. Threads stopped during unload could report garbage after the agent’s runner was gone, leaving a flag set with nothing scheduled, which disabled thread garbage collection in every later session.

iOS

Håvard noticed that CoreDevice’s streaming actions, such as streamapplist, never delivered anything. They push their results as messages flagged as wanting a reply, which Idun’s XPC connection silently dropped unless they were replies themselves. Those are now forwarded, and our Fruity backend acknowledges each one, as devicectl does. Thanks!

GLib

A leak in our GLib is gone. If code on a new thread asks for the current thread before GLib’s own thread entrypoint runs, as an Interceptor hook on libc’s thread entrypoint may, GLib creates a placeholder and queues cleanups on it. The placeholder was then replaced without being destroyed, along with everything it was meant to clean up.

Enjoy!

Changelog
  • agent-container: Share one container across host sessions, fixing a crash when creating a second DeviceManager. Thanks @kkuehl!
  • idun: Release the device monitor’s backends on stop, fixing frida_deinit() hanging while idund is running. Thanks @kkuehl!
  • linux: Keep threads whose registers can’t be read. Thanks @Cassian433 and @JingMatrix!
  • agent: Don’t wedge thread garbage collection on garbage reported during teardown.
  • glib: Adopt the placeholder thread in the thread proxy, fixing a leak.
  • idun: Forward XPC messages that want a reply. Thanks @hsorbo!
  • fruity: Acknowledge XPC messages that want a reply. Thanks @hsorbo!

items.title: Where Deception Fits in a Zero Trust Threat Hunting Framework
items.summary: Key Takeaways Zero Trust controls access, but cannot always identify malicious activity from compromised accounts or legitimate-looking sessions. Deception technology uses decoys and breadcrumbs to expose attackers through high-confidence alerts. Fake credentials and deceptive assets help detect credential theft, reconnaissance, and lateral movement. Integrating deception with network, endpoint, and identity telemetry strengthens threat hunting. Risk-based decoy placement and automated alert correlation improve detection across hybrid, cloud, IoT, and container environments. Combining Zero Trust with deception helps reduce attacker dwell time and limit undetected intrusions. Zero Trust earned its place by rejecting a dangerous assumption: that anything inside the network can be trusted. NIST SP 800-207 [1] says it plainly. It grants no implicit trust based on network location or asset ownership, and authentication and authorization happen before a session starts. CISA’s Zero Trust Maturity Model [2] then gives organizations a staged path to get there. What those controls can’t do is vouch for what happens after a session opens. A valid identity on a healthy-looking device can still belong to an attacker. A threat hunting framework built for 2027 needs evidence that doesn’t depend on every access decision being right. Deception provides that evidence. It places decoys and deceptive credentials where no legitimate user has any reason to go, so any interaction with them is worth investigating. In short, deception belongs where access control stops and behavioral evidence has to take over. Understanding the Visibility Gaps in Zero Trust Security The Zero Trust model rests on a few key principles. Verify explicitly, grant least privilege access, and assume breach. Identity and access management, network segmentation, and strict access controls put those principles into practice by judging each access request on its own merits instead of by where it came from. Each of those controls answers a question about permission. None of them answers whether the activity is malicious. A compromised account passes identity verification because the credentials are real. A malicious insider already holds the access their job requires. A policy engine can be configured flawlessly and still grant access to a genuine identity that someone else is using. The 2026 threat data shows how often attackers skip the front door. Verizon’s 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report [3] , published in May, found that vulnerability exploitation was the leading initial access vector at 31%, ahead of credential abuse at 13%. The report also found that only 26% of vulnerabilities in CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog were fully remediated in 2025, with a median of 43 days to full resolution. An attacker who exploits a flaw arrives without credentials and goes looking for them afterward. Mandiant’s M-Trends 2026 [4] points the same way. Exploits were the top initial infection vector at 32% for the sixth year in a row. Voice phishing rose to second place at 11%, according to the executive edition. Voice phishing aims to get a person to hand over access, which is exactly the case an identity check can’t catch. Third parties widen the exposure further. Verizon reports that breaches involving a third party rose 60% and now account for 48% of the total, so supply chain attacks are a routine path into an organization’s network. Once attackers are inside, east-west traffic is where most of the work happens. Lateral movement between workloads, file shares, and cloud services often uses the same protocols and admin tools as normal operations, so it rarely stands out. Why Threat Hunting Needs to Go Beyond Traditional Zero Trust Controls Enforcing access policies and finding malicious behavior are different jobs. A policy decision returns allow or deny. A hunter has to decide whether an allowed action was part of an intrusion. Hunters usually rely on threat intelligence, historical data, network traffic analysis , and endpoint detection. Each is valuable, and each works by spotting something unusual against a noisy baseline. That is also the weakness, because threat actors who have already gained access work hard to stay inside the baseline. M-Trends 2026 reports a global median dwell time of 14 days, up from 11 the year before. For cyber espionage and North Korean IT worker cases, the median was 122 days. The same report says the median time from initial access to hand-off to a second group fell to 22 seconds in 2025, down from more than eight hours in 2022. Mandiant also estimates that the mean time to exploit has dropped to about negative seven days, which means exploitation often begins before a patch exists. In some intrusions, defenders get seconds before follow-on activity starts. In others, the attacker stays quiet for months. CISA’s maturity model treats visibility and analytics as a cross-cutting capability that runs through every pillar. For hunting teams, the practical lesson is to find indicators that stay reliable when an attacker’s behavior looks legitimate. Where Deception Fits in a Zero Trust Threat Hunting Framework What deception looks like in an enterprise MITRE Engage [5] describes adversary engagement as the use of cyber denial and deception, within strategic planning and analysis, to raise the cost and lower the value of an adversary’s operations. In practice, that means fake assets that are believable enough to attract an attacker, with each one monitored. Fidelis Deception ® builds on two main object types. Decoys duplicate high-value assets such as laptops, servers, routers, printers, and enterprise IoT devices, along with operating systems, services, and applications. In the cloud, they extend to cloud applications, OneDrive, SharePoint, cloud user accounts, and Active Directory users, including Azure AD. Breadcrumbs point toward those decoys from real assets. They include files, documents, emails, memory credentials, registry keys, and canary files. Machine learning then creates decoys from real assets and adjusts where decoys and breadcrumbs sit as risk changes. While an attacker spends time in the deception layer, the real assets and the access to them stay intact. Deception detects only what interacts with it, and an attacker who never touches a decoy won’t trigger it. It works best alongside network, endpoint, and identity telemetry, not in place of them. Next, compare the inventory with your identity and access management and network access controls, and look for blind spots. items.title: ownCloud Infinite Scale 8.2 updates round-up (8.2.1 to 8.2.4)
items.summary: Four ownCloud Infinite Scale 8.2 patch releases, one friendly round-up Between 2 October and 26 November we shipped four maintenance releases for oCIS 8.2. Here’s what changed, what we’d like you to do, and what you can leave alone. If you run ownCloud Infinite Scale (oCIS), you may have noticed a steady stream of patch releases lately. We know that’s a lot of release notes to keep up with, so we’ve pulled the 8.2 line together here. You’ll find what’s new, what we recommend, and what to check before you update. A quick word about 8.0. That line also picked up some security and bug fixes in recent weeks, but we won’t walk through them here. If you’re still on 8.0, skip ahead to the “Still on 8.0?” section below. We’re also testing the 9.0 release candidates, and we cover those in a separate post . The short version On the 8.2 line: update to the latest release, which is 8.2.4 at the time of writing (26 November). Still on 8.0? Please move to the latest 8.2 release, and have a look at our 2.0 post before you start. Two settings may need a look if you’re updating from an earlier 8.2 version. GRPC_MAX_CONNECTION_AGE is replaced by new keepalive settings (8.2.1). And if you run multi-instance oCIS with LDAP, you need an explicit OCIS_LDAP_USER_FILTER (8.2.2). Copying our Collabora examples? Four ownCloud Infinite Scale 8.2 patch releases, one friendly round-up

Between 2 October and 26 November we shipped four maintenance releases for oCIS 8.2. Here’s what changed, what we’d like you to do, and what you can leave alone.

If you run ownCloud Infinite Scale (oCIS), you may have noticed a steady stream of patch releases lately. We know that’s a lot of release notes to keep up with, so we’ve pulled the 8.2 line together here. You’ll find what’s new, what we recommend, and what to check before you update.

A quick word about 8.0. That line also picked up some security and bug fixes in recent weeks, but we won’t walk through them here. If you’re still on 8.0, skip ahead to the “Still on 8.0?” section below. We’re also testing the 9.0 release candidates, and we cover those in a separate post.

The short version
  • On the 8.2 line: update to the latest release, which is 8.2.4 at the time of writing (26 November).
  • Still on 8.0? Please move to the latest 8.2 release, and have a look at our 2.0 post before you start.
  • Two settings may need a look if you’re updating from an earlier 8.2 version. GRPC_MAX_CONNECTION_AGE is replaced by new keepalive settings (8.2.1). And if you run multi-instance oCIS with LDAP, you need an explicit OCIS_LDAP_USER_FILTER (8.2.2).
  • Copying our Collabora examples? From 8.2.4 they need admin credentials in your .env
  • Planning ahead: the owncloudsql and posixfs storage drivers, along with their environment variables, are scheduled for removal in oCIS 9.0.0. We announced this with 8.2.3.
Still on 8.0?

If you’re still running the 8.0 line, our advice is simple: move to the latest 8.2 release, which is 8.2.4 at the time of writing. The 8.0 line also received some security and bug fixes recently, and we won’t go through them one by one, because those fixes live on in the newer lines. More generally, we’d encourage everyone in the community to move to the newest version as soon as it’s available. Our focus is on the latest release, and we can’t keep several stable branches going at once.

Moving from 8.0 to 8.2 takes a little care, so please read our 8.2.0 release post before you start. Two things in it are worth checking. First, the default for OIDC group auto-provisioning has changed. If your deployment relies on groups coming from your OIDC provider, you’ll need to set PROXY_AUTOPROVISION_CLAIM_GROUPS explicitly after upgrading, or group memberships from your provider will stop being synced at login. Second, self-service password changes now go through a dedicated endpoint, which matters if you have scripts or integrations that change passwords. The other new settings in 8.2.0 (two switches for turning off public or direct sharing, and an optional audience check for OIDC tokens) keep today’s behaviour until you change them. The 8.2.1 and 8.2.2 notes below apply to you as well.

2 October: 8.2.1

On the security side, 8.2.1 updates the gRPC library to close a denial-of-service issue in how gRPC servers handle certain connections. It also updates an image-decoding library, refreshes the Go toolchain and other dependencies, and strengthens protection against repeated password guessing on password-protected public links.

A few fixes are worth knowing about:

  • Running share operations at the same time could corrupt share metadata, and that’s fixed.
  • LDAP instance lookups are now cached, which saves repeated round-trips to your directory.
  • A brief hiccup at your OIDC provider now produces a retryable “service unavailable” answer instead of an authentication error, so clients no longer read it as a failed login.
  • Deleting a space also accepts an X-Purge header, for clients that send it that way.

GRPC_MAX_CONNECTION_AGE is replaced (not kept alongside) by client-side keepalive, which you tune with GRPC_CLIENT_KEEPALIVE_TIME and GRPC_CLIENT_KEEPALIVE_TIMEOUT. Keepalive pings stay off unless you set those variables. TLS is now available for NATS store and registry connections and for the frontend’s stat cache store connection. The janitor that cleans up expired public shares is now configurable with OCIS_SHARING_ENABLE_EXPIRED_SHARES_CLEANUP and OCIS_SHARING_JANITOR_RUN_INTERVAL. Under heavy load, requests waiting on a share cache lock now give up once the client has gone, so abandoned requests no longer pile up and hold on to memory. And the Collabora examples in ocis_full and ocis_ocm are hardened: Collabora is restricted to the hosts it needs, runs on its own internal network, and the admin console requires credentials. If you copy those examples, please set COLLABORA_ADMIN_USER and COLLABORA_ADMIN_PASSWORD in your .env file.

No breaking changes are listed for 8.2.4, apart from the example Collabora setup needing those credentials.

Getting the update with Docker

If you run the official image, pulling the latest 8.2 release is a single command:

docker pull owncloud/ocis:8.2.4

The image page is on Docker Hub. If you’d rather pin another exact version, use its full tag.

A short checklist before you update
  • Back up your data and configuration, as you would for any update.
  • If you rely on GRPC_MAX_CONNECTION_AGE, move to GRPC_CLIENT_KEEPALIVE_TIME and GRPC_CLIENT_KEEPALIVE_TIMEOUT.
  • If you run multi-instance oCIS with LDAP, set OCIS_LDAP_USER_FILTER before updating to 8.2.2 or later.
  • If you copy our Collabora examples, set COLLABORA_ADMIN_USER and COLLABORA_ADMIN_PASSWORD in your .env
  • Check whether any of your configuration uses the OWNCLOUDSQL or POSIX environment variables.
  • Coming from 8.0? Read our 2.0 post first, and check how your deployment handles OIDC groups and password changes.
Looking ahead

oCIS 9.0 is on its way, and we’d love your help testing it. Our 9.0 release candidate post covers what’s inside and how to try it. If something doesn’t look right after an update, tell us. You can open an issue on GitHub or start a thread on ownCloud Central, and we’ll happily help.

Thank you for running ownCloud, and for telling us when things go sideways. It makes every release better.

Warmly,
The ownCloud team

Attackers are exploiting a second critical flaw in Drupal, the content management system (CMS) behind many government, university, corporate, and media websites. Site owners are responsible for applying the fix. For visitors, a hijacked site can put personal data and devices at risk.

On November 18, Drupal released a patch for a remote code execution (RCE) flaw, CVE-2026-132165. The flaw could let attackers take over a site by abusing Drupal’s installer file, install.php. Drupal’s security team received a report of attacks on live sites as early as November 19.

  • No login is needed. Anonymous attackers can exploit the first flaw. They can attempt to reinstall Drupal and gain control of the site or run code on the server.

  • Already exploited. CISA added the first flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog and gave federal agencies until November 27 to fix it.
  • Drupal has a history of abuse. CISA has flagged six Drupal flaws as exploited since November 2021. Two of them were used in ransomware attacks.

items.title: Hackers Set Freezer Controls to 100°C, Then Lock Technicians Out of the System
items.summary: Hackers changed a freezer chamber’s temperature setting to 100°C at Salamerija Alpija, a meat processing plant in Tolmin, Slovenia. When a service technician tried to sign in to the cooling control system, his access was blocked. Instead of the controls, his screen showed a photo of Italian minister Matteo Salvini with a caption that translates as “Thank Uncle Matteo,” cooperative director Nikola Šavle told Slovenian news outlet 24ur . The freezer did not reach 100°C. That was the setting entered in the control system, not the temperature measured inside the chamber. Šavle said staff caught the change before temperatures rose and no meat products spoiled. The Tolmin Agricultural Cooperative estimated that about €250,000 worth of goods could have been lost. That figure represents stock at risk, not a confirmed financial loss. Hackers Changed Freezer Temperature The first sign of trouble came around noon, when an employee noticed the 100°C setting during a check at the salami plant. Staff knew about recent attacks on supermarket refrigeration systems across Europe , so they checked cooling equipment at other cooperative sites. They found another problem at the slaughterhouse and discovered that a refrigerator at one of their stores had been set to 20°C instead of its usual 2–3°C. The cooperative managed temperatures across its cold rooms and chambers through an internet-connected system. Staff disconnected the cooling equipment from the network and set the temperatures manually. The technician’s blocked login meant the team could not rely on the usual computer interface to restore the settings. The public report does not explain how his login was blocked or whether anyone had changed his account settings. The cooperative’s alarm was designed to warn staff about an unexpected drop in temperature. This time, Šavle said the target appeared to have been changed in the digital system, and staff received no warning. The distinction matters: an alarm that watches the temperature inside a room may not tell staff that someone has changed the target the equipment follows. The cooperative added in-person checks, with staff due to review settings every few hours. Šavle questioned what would have happened on a weekend, when production sites are not staffed. The cooperative said it planned to report the incident to Slovenia’s national cyber response center, SI-CERT. The Slovenian Press Agency also reported the attack . The Tolmin incident shares a visible feature with attacks on European supermarkets: someone changed cooling settings without permission. That does not establish that the same people were responsible or that they used the same equipment or method. The Salvini image also does not establish who was behind the attack or why they targeted the plant. Separately, the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency published a November 24 advisory on Danfoss commercial refrigeration controllers . The Tolmin report did not identify the controller maker or model, explain how the attackers got in, or name a suspect. There is no public evidence in that report linking the Danfoss flaw to the incident. Refrigeration controllers are part of operational technology, the equipment and software that monitor or control physical processes. For food producers, a useful starting point is an inventory of operational technology assets . It should show which controller serves each room, who can change its settings, and how outside service teams connect. CISA’s guidance for operational technology operators recommends removing direct access from the public internet, separating control equipment from business networks, and using strong sign-in controls where remote access is necessary. It also recommends practicing manual operation so staff can keep equipment running safely if they lose remote access. Operators can use an independent sensor to warn staff when a room leaves its approved temperature range, regardless of what the controller is set to. A separate alert for an unexpected change to the target can flag trouble before the room warms. Both alerts need to reach someone who can act outside normal working hours. In Tolmin, a routine walk-through caught what the alarm did not. The test for another cold storage operator is whether the same change would wake someone on a Sunday, and whether that person could restore safe settings without logging in remotely. items.title: 12-Year-Old NFS2ROOT Linux Flaw Let Hackers Take Full Control of Servers Without a Password
items.summary: A critical Linux kernel flaw called NFS2ROOT could let an attacker take full control of an unpatched Network File System (NFS) server without logging in. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-99362 , affects the Linux kernel’s NFS server when NFSv4.1 or NFSv4.2 is enabled and an attacker can reach TCP port 2049. The affected code dates back to Linux 3.16, released in 2014. OpenSec Intelligence gave the flaw a severity score of 9.8 out of 10 and showed what it could do in a controlled test. In its November 25 video demonstration , a separate machine connects to the test server and causes it to run commands with root privileges. The server then shuts down. OpenSec says it has kept the exploit private. The video shows that remote root access was possible in the tested setup, but does not establish that attackers have used the flaw in the wild. NFS2ROOT Linux Vulnerability NFS2ROOT Remote Root Exploitation Overview (Image Source: Opensec) NFS lets computers access files stored on another machine. The affected Linux service nfsd , runs inside the kernel rather than as an ordinary application. It caches recent replies so that if a client retries a request, the server can return the same answer without doing the work again. The flaw lies in how the server decides whether a reply fits in that cache. An affected server can treat an incomplete reply as a success and try to store it in a buffer that is too small. The resulting write spills beyond the space set aside for the reply and can damage nearby kernel data. This is known as a heap overflow. The fix makes the server check that there is enough room and report an error when the reply cannot fit. Unlike the Copy Fail Linux kernel flaw , NFS2ROOT does not require an attacker to already have local access. Session Reply-Cache Heap Overflow Diagram (Image Source: Opensec) OpenSec credits Jérémy Jean of France’s national cybersecurity agency, ANSSI, with submitting an upstream fix in August 2026. OpenSec says its automated research tool, Antara, independently found the flaw and built the working demonstration. The company notified Linux kernel security staff and NFS maintainers in September. The official CVE record lists November 19 as the publication date. Check Linux file servers, network-attached storage appliances, build servers, and storage nodes that serve NFS shares to Kubernetes workloads. A Linux machine that only mounts a remote share as a client does not expose this server flaw by doing so. NFS2ROOT is also separate from the Kubernetes NFS CSI driver vulnerability , which involved how the driver handled directory paths rather than how the Linux kernel’s NFS server handled replies. Kernel Warning and KASLR Leak (Image Source: Opensec) On a Linux NFS server, cat /proc/fs/nfsd/versions shows whether +4.1 or +4.2 is enabled. The command ss -ltn 'sport = :2049' shows whether the host is listening on TCP port 2049. A listening port does not tell you which machines can reach it. Review firewall rules and cloud security groups to check access from other network segments. A file server does not need to face the public internet to be reachable from a compromised machine on the internal network. Confirmed Remote Root Shell Execution (Image Source: Opensec) The official list of fixed kernel versions includes Linux 5.10.275, 5.15.226, 6.1.193, 6.6.163, 6.12.117, 6.18.61, 7.3.2, and 7.4-rc1. For a distribution kernel or storage appliance, check the vendor’s advisory for CVE-2026-99362 rather than relying on the version number alone. Vendors can apply the fix to an older kernel branch without adopting the upstream release number. After installing the update, reboot and run uname -r to confirm the system is running the updated kernel. If you cannot patch immediately, limit access to TCP port 2049 to machines that need it. OpenSec also recommends disabling NFSv4.1 and NFSv4.2 where workloads allow it. Check client requirements before restarting the NFS service, since disabling those versions can remove features that storage workloads depend on. Treat both steps as temporary measures, not substitutes for patching. For systems that were reachable before patching, OpenSec’s detection guidance points to kernel warnings involving nfsd4_check_resp_size , unexpected shells started by kernel workers, and bursts of short NFSv4.1 sessions from one source. These are leads, not proof of compromise. Compare the timestamps with network and process logs, and prioritize any unexplained commands that ran with root privileges. items.title: Hackers Break Into U.S. Air Force Cloud Platform Used to Manage Military Operations and Data
items.summary: Hackers broke into Cloud One, the U.S. Air Force’s main cloud computing platform, putting sensitive military, personnel, and logistics data at risk. Three people familiar with the breach told Reuters about the intrusion. Two said it was discovered during upgrade work within roughly a month of the November 27 report. It was not determined who was behind the breach, how far the intruders got, or whether they stole any data. Hackers Break Into U.S. Air Force Cloud Platform The discovery disrupted work across Cloud One. The Air Force paused plans to move back-office applications onto the platform, and updates to applications already running there were blocked. One source told Reuters that some users lost administrator access. Another said investigators brought in U.S. Cyber Command to assess the damage. Cyber Command did not respond to requests for comment. Another source told Reuters that the attackers used a software flaw to reach the control plane, the layer administrators use to manage cloud services and access. Reuters could not identify the flaw. The level of access matters because reaching the management layer is not the same as gaining access to every application or record it supports. The report did not establish which permissions the intruders gained or what they did with them. The source said the access could, in theory, let intruders check whether military aircraft were operational or follow the movement of spare parts. Reuters did not establish that either happened. The case differs from the separate Pentagon personnel data breach disclosed in September, when defense officials confirmed that unauthorized users had accessed a system holding personal information on more than three million people. The Air Force launched Cloud One in 2017 to give military applications a common home across commercial cloud services from Microsoft, Amazon, Oracle, and Alphabet. The Air Force’s Cloud One site describes it as a shared platform for Defense Department applications. It hosts software for personnel records, payroll, maintenance, and logistics, alongside systems that support military operations. One of those systems, Cloud-Based Command and Control, combines air defense radar and other feeds from across North America. The figure indicates the range of the munitions tracking system, not the number of sites that were breached. Reuters did not confirm that the intruders accessed either application. The update freeze left Air Force staff unable to apply fixes to applications already on Cloud One, Reuters reported. That is a separate problem from the paused migrations: one slows the move to the cloud, while the other affects software already in use. T he Air Force told Reuters it does not discuss the security or operating status of specific systems. It did not confirm the breach in its statement. Cloud audit logs can help investigators distinguish what an account could access from what it actually did. As Cyber Security News reported in its coverage of CISA’s cloud logging playbook , records of user and administrator activity can help trace a breach. For Cloud One, the most important questions remain: which systems the intruders reached, whether they changed or copied anything, and when the Air Force can safely resume updates. Researchers demonstrated that temporary resource-exhaustion conditions can make the installer incorrectly conclude that an existing site is not installed, reopening setup functionality to an anonymous remote attacker. Contact Sales Searchlight Cyber demonstrated the attack against Drupal 8.9, 9, 10, and 11 using Apache or PHP-FPM with both MySQL and PostgreSQL. The researchers also showed a path from installer takeover to arbitrary PHP execution by abusing Drupal’s SQLite installation option. The risk has increased further because Drupal disclosed a related follow-up issue, CVE-2026-136716, on November 25. That flaw affects certain sites left in unusual or incomplete installation states after the original fixes and is also being exploited in the wild. Drupal therefore recommends updating to the newest supported core release, running update.php, and explicitly blocking public access to the installer. Drupal 8 and Drupal 9 are already end-of-life, while Drupal 10.5.x and Drupal 11.2.x or earlier no longer receive security coverage. The underlying issue stems from Drupal’s handling of failure conditions inside its installation process. Drupal normally performs checks before allowing the installer to continue on an already configured website. These checks are intended to determine whether a database configuration exists and whether the site has already completed installation. Searchlight Cyber researchers found that temporary system-level resource exhaustion can make those checks fail in a sequence that Drupal interprets incorrectly. The demonstrated attack follows a FAIL → FAIL → SUCCESS pattern. First, the attacker deliberately causes an early database connection to fail. A subsequent check intended to determine whether Drupal already has an existing installation also fails. Drupal interprets those failures as evidence that it may be dealing with a new, unconfigured website. The attacker then allows a later database connectivity operation to succeed within the same installation workflow. If the timing is correct, Drupal proceeds into installer forms that should never have become accessible on an established production system. Drupal’s installation workflow can then write those database settings into settings.php, causing the live site to use the attacker-controlled database. items.summary: Today's links Taylorism and AI's shared sales-pitch : Bosses will buy anything if they think it'll give them more control over their workers. Hey look at this : Delights to delectate. Object permanence : UK recordings copyright won't go to 95 years; McDonald's sandwich patent; McLaren's son torches punk tat; Chestburster turkey; O(N^2) nationalism. Upcoming appearances : Virtual, Oxford, Santa Barbara, Montreal. Recent appearances : Where I've been. Latest books : You keep readin' em, I'll keep writin' 'em. Upcoming books : Like I said, I'll keep writin' 'em. Colophon : All the rest. Taylorism and AI's shared sales-pitch ( permalink ) More than a century ago, the most powerful, wealthiest men in the world fell for a con-artist named Frederick Winslow Taylor, who sold them expensive consulting services to help them apply "Scientific Management" to their companies: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Winslow_Taylor Upon receipt of eye-popping consulting fees, Taylor dispatched unqualified young men in "scientist" drag (lab coats, clipboards, stopwatches) to fan out over factory floors. These smart young men noted how much time each worker at each station took to perform each task, then "optimized" each worker using a homebrew choreographer's notation that showed the "correct" way to make each motion and set an upper bound for how many seconds it should take to perform each task. Notably, these "scientists" refused to discuss their findings with the workers they observed: they never asked why a worker made a specific motion or tackled a task in a certain way. The workers were presumed to be ploddingly unreflective about their jobs (at best), or malicious featherbedders who were stealing from the boss by slacking off (at worst). Either way, Taylor's "scientists" could see no reason to discuss their findings with the workers. The job of the "scientists" was to transform those workers into a well-oiled machine, and no one but a blockhead would ask a piston or a gear why it chose to move the way it did. To use a technical term, these "scientists" were fucking idiots and their recommendations were (to use another technical term) bullshit . Not only did they set impossible quotas for workers, they were also notably bad at choreography and routinely required workers to move in ways that resulted in early fatigue and high rates of injury. Wherever Taylor's "scientists" went, morale plunged, labor unrest surged, and the business was made worse off. Which all raises a question: why would the owners of these businesses – who had the intelligence and self-interest to build up extremely profitable enterprises – throw away their money and kneecap their firms on this charlatanry? The answer lies in the psychology of Taylor's sales-pitch. Taylor's marks owed their fortunes and power to their ability to scale up their firms to sizes never before seen, thanks to innovations like the assembly line and to exogenous factors like mechanized transportation and long-distance telecommunications, which let them address much larger markets than their predecessors. The downside to this was a large workforce (too large to keep individual tabs on) that was spread out over a large factory floor or complex (too large to constantly observe). A compromised ad account can give criminals a trusted business identity and a way to pay for more ads. The Chrome extension can permanently delete selected emails, potentially hiding warnings that would otherwise prompt the owner to act. One ad reached more than 6,000 people, though that figure measures ad reach, not infections. The ads sent users to download sites serving a roughly 74 MB ZIP archive. items.title: Hackers Use Hidden Chrome Extension to Read Gmail Messages Without Stealing Passwords
items.summary: Hackers using Remus Stealer can read unread Gmail messages without stealing the victim’s Google password. The Windows malware installs a Chrome extension disguised as Google Sheets, then uses the Gmail session already open in the browser. The victim does not have to open a message for the extension to collect it, putting private conversations, sign-in codes, and password reset links at risk. The findings undercut the operators’ claim that they had a Gmail zero-day, or a previously unknown security flaw. Researchers found no evidence that the extension could keep collecting new messages after Google revoked the session. The real danger comes later: a password reset does not remove the extension, and signing back in on the infected computer can give it access again. Hudson Rock analysts writing for InfoStealers noted the malicious extension in a November 24 update, crediting Invoke RE and Gen Threat Labs with identifying and analyzing it. Their earlier investigation examined screenshots of a mailbox viewer and interviewed the developer and a self-described customer. Those screenshots showed what the panel displayed, not whether it could retrieve fresh mail after account recovery. Hackers Use Hidden Chrome Extension The Gmail feature is one part of a broader Windows malware operation. Earlier reporting on Remus browser data theft documented its ability to collect saved passwords, cookies, and cryptocurrency wallet data. Gen Threat Labs found that the Gmail interception module was not present in every build it examined, so a Remus infection does not automatically mean the extension was installed. The add-on identifies itself as Google Sheets, version 0.5.4 , and claims to offer offline document editing. Researchers found no spreadsheet interface. A Pinterest verification message displayed in the advertised Mail interception interface (Source – Infostealer) As detailed in coverage of the fake Google Sheets extension , it loads from local files rather than through a normal Chrome Web Store installation. In the analyzed setup, Chrome showed it as an unpacked extension and had Developer Mode enabled. While Chrome is running and Gmail is signed in, the extension checks for unread mail about once a minute across up to ten account slots in the affected profile. Ten slots does not mean ten accounts were compromised. Researchers observed it retrieving full messages and sending the sender, subject, message body, and recipient’s address to an attacker-controlled server. They did not observe it sending attachments. This differs from browser session cookie theft , where an attacker can copy login data and try to reuse it elsewhere. Remus’s Gmail extension instead relies on the browser to make requests within the victim’s existing session. It does not defeat Google’s two-step verification at sign-in, but it can expose codes or recovery links that other services send to the inbox. Why a Gmail Password Reset Is Not Enough Revoking the active session stops the extension from reading new mail, but it does not erase messages already copied or remove the malicious code from Chrome. That distinction also matters when investigating other malicious browser extensions : securing the account and cleaning the device address different parts of the incident. Do not sign back in on the affected computer until the underlying infection has been removed. A populated inbox view (Source – Infostealer) For a confirmed infection, isolate the computer and preserve the extension files, Chrome profile settings, and relevant logs. From a separate, trusted device, change exposed passwords, revoke affected sessions, and review connected apps and recovery settings. Check Gmail forwarding rules, filters, and delegated access for unauthorized changes. Prioritize other accounts that use the inbox for password resets or verification, especially if their messages arrived during the suspected exposure window. New research from Gen Threat Labs traced the supposed Gmail “zero-day” to a Chrome extension that masquerades as Google Sheets. The malicious extension stays installed after a password change and can start reading your mail again when you sign back in on the infected device. On November 8, the developers of the Remus infostealer began advertising a Gmail “zero-day.” They said it gave access to a victim’s mailbox even after they changed their password and signed out of all sessions. Gen Threat Labs published its findings on November 24. The researchers found no email-stealing code in the main stealer. That lives in a separate module that Remus downloads from the attackers’ server when the malware runs. The developers advertised the feature as exclusive to their $1,000-a-month Enterprise tier. The module is a native DLL whose only job is to install a malicious extension in Google Chrome, the only browser it targets. It edits the victim’s Chrome profile files to register the extension and recalculates the integrity checks that protect those files. It also turns on Developer mode , which Chrome requires to run unpacked extensions. The extension calls itself “Google Sheets” and copies the description of the Google Docs Offline extension. It requests access to all websites. Every minute, it checks Gmail for unread messages, retrieves the contents, and then sends the subject, body, sender, and your email address to the attackers. So, the password change claim is true? Only partly. When you sign out or end your Gmail session, the extension stops reading your mail. But it stays installed in Chrome. As soon as you sign back in on the infected device with your new password, it can start reading your mail again. You might never notice it. The visible clues are a new extension card and the Developer mode switch turned on. But it’s still a persistence trick and a marketing pitch, not a Google vulnerability. Malware able to install an extension silently could just as easily steal your session cookies directly. Which doesn’t make it any less dangerous. Especially when your inbox holds password-reset links and verification codes for your other accounts. What to do If you think your device may be infected with an infostealer: Clean the device. The extension can start reading your mail again if you sign back in on the infected computer. Scan with an up-to-date anti-malware solution , and use a separate, clean device to change your Google password. Check your extensions. Enter chrome://extensions in your address bar. Look for extensions you don’t recognize or no longer use. The fake “Google Sheets” extension is marked as unpacked, meaning it was loaded from local files. Google’s real Docs Offline extension is only available from the Chrome Web Store. Remove anything suspicious. Check Developer Mode. In this article
  • Remus malware installs a Chrome extension disguised as Google Sheets
  • The extension can resume stealing unread Gmail messages when you sign back in on the infected device
  • If you suspect an infection, check your Chrome extensions and secure your Google Account from a clean device

In our earlier post about Remus, we covered the claim that the infostealer could read your Gmail even after you changed your password. New research from Gen Threat Labs traced the supposed Gmail “zero-day” to a Chrome extension that masquerades as Google Sheets. The malicious extension stays installed after a password change and can start reading your mail again when you sign back in on the infected device.

On November 8, the developers of the Remus infostealer began advertising a Gmail “zero-day.” They said it gave access to a victim’s mailbox even after they changed their password and signed out of all sessions.

Gen Threat Labs published its findings on November 24. The researchers found no email-stealing code in the main stealer. That lives in a separate module that Remus downloads from the attackers’ server when the malware runs. The developers advertised the feature as exclusive to their $1,000-a-month Enterprise tier.

The module is a native DLL whose only job is to install a malicious extension in Google Chrome, the only browser it targets. It edits the victim’s Chrome profile files to register the extension and recalculates the integrity checks that protect those files. It also turns on Developer mode, which Chrome requires to run unpacked extensions.

The extension calls itself “Google Sheets” and copies the description of the Google Docs Offline extension. It requests access to all websites. Every minute, it checks Gmail for unread messages, retrieves the contents, and then sends the subject, body, sender, and your email address to the attackers.

So, the password change claim is true?

Only partly. When you sign out or end your Gmail session, the extension stops reading your mail. But it stays installed in Chrome. As soon as you sign back in on the infected device with your new password, it can start reading your mail again.

You might never notice it. The visible clues are a new extension card and the Developer mode switch turned on. But it’s still a persistence trick and a marketing pitch, not a Google vulnerability. Malware able to install an extension silently could just as easily steal your session cookies directly. Which doesn’t make it any less dangerous. Especially when your inbox holds password-reset links and verification codes for your other accounts.

If you think your device may be infected with an infostealer:

  • Clean the device. The extension can start reading your mail again if you sign back in on the infected computer. Scan with an up-to-date anti-malware solution, and use a separate, clean device to change your Google password.

The fake “Google Sheets” extension is marked as unpacked, meaning it was loaded from local files. Google’s real Docs Offline extension is only available from the Chrome Web Store. Remove anything suspicious.

items.title: Recent Outages Have Economic Causes
items.summary: This essay originally appeared in The Guardian . It’s an expanded version of the one I posted as “ We Get the Infrastructure We Pay For .” It’s been a bad week for our computerized infrastructure. We’ve seen outages at Microsoft , the FAA , a handful of banks , United Airlines , an unnamed classified NSA network , and Apple . People should be forgiven for suspecting a coordinated cyberattack, a common cause, or at least a conspiracy. But there is none. The incidents are unrelated. They’re not the result of any cyberattack, coordinated or not. And, even more surprising, they don’t seem to be the result of AI. (We can’t say anything about the NSA; we’ll probably never know the details of that one.) It’s really just a series of unfortunate coincidences. None of them should surprise, though. Our computerized infrastructure is both vulnerable and fragile. Much of it is old and has been incrementally patched and upgraded over the decades. A surprising amount of it is maintained by hobbyists, without any recompense. There often aren’t good backup systems. And more and more of it is centralized, meaning that individual failures have cascading consequences across many different aspects of our lives and society. A lot of our tech infrastructure just barely works. And when it fails, it can fail badly. It’s the very opposite of resilience. There are a lot of technological reasons why this is true, but they are all downstream from the economic ones. The technologies we rely on are built and maintained within our economic system—and that’s where the core problems lie. Security, safety, resilience, redundancy and recoverability are all essential parts of reliable technology, but they are all costs. More importantly, they are costs that don’t generate near-term profits. Modern shareholder capitalism, and private equity in particular, prioritizes near-term profits over everything else. This squeezes all apparent inefficiencies—and, additionally, all other positive intangibles—out of a company in pursuit of those profits. Market competition, essential for the forces that nudge companies to provide better services, is another perceived inefficiency. Monopolization removes it in pursuit of near-term profits. From the perspective of a quarterly budget, spending on reliability measures is an inefficiency. They’re expenses that don’t generate revenue. They feel wasteful … until something bad happens. But, if you’re lucky, you can push the costs of failure on to society, further increasing profits. So, we get stranded in airports when planes don’t fly, or have to deal with the fallout when we can’t withdraw money from our bank accounts. The effects of those economic pressures are brittle systems, with single points of failure and cascading failure modes. They’re more susceptible to cyberattack—both human and AI-fueled—and more susceptible to random mistakes. The more we allow unregulated capitalism to privatize gains while socializing risks, the more we should expect these sorts of failures. Upgrading our computerized systems, increasing their reliability, removing single points of failure, and making them more resilient are all technical problems. But they won’t happen until we fix the political and economic ones. We need to change the economic incentives that make it profitable to operate these systems just at the edge of functionality, and to push the costs of failure on to all of us. Fixing that requires regulation—with enforcement and meaningful fines—and stringent antitrust enforcement. But while that’s all easy to say, it’s much harder to implement —especially in the US where monied interests have such a tight hold on the legislative agenda. Until this changes, we should expect lots more of these sorts of failures in the future.

items.title: 3,089 Telegram Job Posts Uncovered in Suspected Spy Recruitment Campaigns
items.summary: A Telegram account offered readers in a Hebrew-language sports group 1,500 shekels for one night’s work. The same ad appeared at precisely 9:43:01 p.m. on 51 days. The account later promoted what looked like a part-time job with a U.S. environmental consultancy. The two offers helped researchers connect ordinary-looking gig ads to a wider set of suspected spy recruitment campaigns. Investigators counted 3,089 recruitment posts from 88 accounts between August 2, 2024, and October 26, 2026. The ads reached Telegram communities in Israel, the Gulf, Europe and the United States, appearing in job boards, student groups and political discussions. Some openly claimed to recruit for Iranian intelligence; others offered paid work without mentioning Iran. The total counts posts, not individual job offers or people recruited. Researchers from Group-IB identified links between the accounts, ads and recruitment contacts, but did not report finding malware. Their November 26 research report examined public Telegram posts, not private replies, payments or completed assignments. Group-IB did not independently attribute the campaigns to Iran or any other state actor. 3,089 Telegram Job Posts Uncovered The biggest jump came in March 2026. Researchers recorded 1,424 posts that month, up from 91 in February, a nearly sixteenfold increase that coincided with the launch of Operation Epic Fury on February 28. One account published 1,028 of the March posts. The report establishes when the surge happened, but does not establish who ordered it or why. Tracking the accounts behind the ads revealed what a keyword search would have missed. Of the 3,089 posts, 1,271, or about 41%, contained neither an explicit reference to Iran nor an Iran-branded recruitment contact. VIPEmployment’s Telegram profile, claiming to represent an intelligence service and promising recruits ‘a safe and secure atmosphere’ (Source – Group-IB) Earlier reporting on Iranian fake job offers documented a separate campaign built around bogus recruitment websites. In this case, researchers found the connection by looking at what the same Telegram accounts promoted over time. One channel copied the name and logo of SWCA Environmental Consultants, a legitimate U.S. company. It initially asked readers to report pollution and later offered payment in U.S. dollars for inspecting locations it selected. From May 27 to July 7, one account posted 580 ads for the channel across 46 groups in Hebrew, Russian, Uzbek and English. Group-IB found no evidence that the real company was involved. 673 posts classified as alerts Researchers also found recruitment contacts tucked into conflict updates and posts styled as breaking news. They identified 29 placements marked as advertising across seven open-source intelligence channels. In a separate set of 673 posts classified as alerts or demoralizing content, 476 carried a recruitment contact. As with Telegram political influence campaigns , the context matters: a reader who joined for news could encounter a pitch without ever visiting a job board. For investigators, the useful signal is an overlap: the same contact appearing in otherwise unrelated ads, identical wording across renamed accounts, or posts arriving on a regular schedule. A display name alone is not enough. On March 5, 2026, Ali_vqy posted an Arabic recruitment appeal claiming to represent ‘Iran’s intelligence service,’ followed 172 seconds later by a Hebrew-language field-research job advertisement (Source – Group-IB) For job seekers, the warning sign is not Telegram itself. It is an employer you cannot verify offering unusually high pay for unclear work, then asking for location proof, footage or identity documents. As with other Telegram job recruitment scams , verify the employer using contact details you find independently. If you have already responded and the recruiter pressures or threatens you, stop taking assignments, preserve the messages if safe, and seek help from local authorities. Impersonation channel SWCA Israel / SWCAil Used the branding of a legitimate consultancy without evidence of its involvement. Account display name Alexis Ramos Promoted both the environmental pitch and a separate paid-task channel. Posting pattern 21:43:01 on 51 days The same account repeatedly posted the same ad in one sports group. File hashes Not published The report did not identify a malware sample to hash. items.title: Tor Browser Flaw Could Reveal Users’ Real IP Addresses With Just One Click on Malicious Websites
items.summary: A malicious website could expose a Tor Browser user’s public IP address with a single click, according to research published by security firm Calif on November 26, 2026. Researcher Carlos Roque demonstrated the attack against Tor Browser 15.0.22 on Linux with default settings. The Tor Project had already shipped the fix in Tor Browser 15.0.23 on September 15, more than two months before the research became public. The click happened after the user opened the malicious page. In Calif’s test, simply loading the page was not enough. The report shows what was possible on the tested build, not that Tor users were targeted in a live campaign. There were no confirmed reports of attacks using the flaw at the time of disclosure. Tor Browser normally sends web traffic through a series of relays. An ordinary website sees the IP address of the final relay, known as the exit relay, rather than the public address behind the user’s connection. Calif’s test showed that the browser could still load the page through Tor while making a separate connection that bypassed the network. The server receiving that second connection could see its public source IP address. Tor Browser Flaw The attack started with CVE-2026-92027, a memory bug in Gecko, the Firefox engine that Tor Browser uses. The bug is called a use-after-free because the browser keeps using a piece of memory after releasing it. In Calif’s demonstration, that flaw was the first step in a chain that caused the browser to make a direct connection. The researchers did not need to break Tor’s encryption or take control of a relay. The address exposed was the one the direct connection used to reach the internet. Depending on the user’s setup, that could be a home network’s public IP address or a VPN server’s address. It would not, on its own, reveal the user’s name. The finding follows separate reports of a Firefox engine flaw that affected Tor Browser and a one-click browser extension flaw patched in Tails . Neither was part of Calif’s demonstration. The Tor Project’s September release notes show that version 15.0.23 moved to Firefox 140.16.0 ESR, the extended support version of Firefox. Calif confirmed that 15.0.23 stopped the attack it demonstrated. Users still running 15.0.22 should install the latest stable release for their platform rather than stop at the September patch. Use the browser’s built-in updater or the official Tor Browser download page. The September release also noted a separate Windows installer issue. An expired code-signing certificate caused warnings on some fresh installs. However, the browser’s automatic updates used a different signing key. That warning did not indicate an IP leak. If an old installer still shows a signature warning, get a fresh copy from the Tor Project rather than bypassing it. After updating, restart the browser and check that it is no longer running the affected version. What Are Leading Organizations Doing About AI and Cyber Risks? Find Out. View Details!

items.summary: Recently I was taking another look at one of my perennial favourite Kubernetes security problems, the lack of certificate revocation and, with some agentic assistance, I realised there’s a kind of hacky approach that will work to mitigating some of the risks of using client certificate authentication in Kubernetes. Background One of the challenges of using Kubernetes is that none of the in-built authentication methods are suitable for production use, meaning that anyone using Kubernetes has to implement their own authentication, generally by tying it to an external IAM source like cloud IAM or an LDAP directory. This isn’t ideal for smaller orgs, which leaves them looking for the “least bad” alternative, which is client certificates. In many ways client certificates aren’t a bad form of authentication, but a major headache in Kubernetes is the lack of certificate revocation support. This is a known issue going back to 2015, but at the moment there’s no official solution. Hacking up a fix So if we want to use client certificate authentication how do we fix this problem? Well since Kubernetes v1.32, when a request is authenticated with a client certificate, the API server attaches a credential ID to the user’s information, in the authentication.kubernetes.io/credential-id extra field. This isn’t something stored in the certificate itself, it’s calculated by the API server as a SHA-256 hash of the certificate ( X509SHA256= ), which means that every client certificate can be uniquely identified, even ones that were issued long before v1.32. This opens up the idea that if we can intercept authorization decisions in the API server, we can have a mechanism to revoke access by marking a specific credential ID as revoked. As a proof of concept I knocked up a tool called certrevoker which works as an operator in a Kubernetes cluster. This is very much a proof of concept, so don’t deploy it in a production cluster without a lot of improvement :D The first stage is to keep track of the client certificates that exist in the cluster, as Kubernetes doesn’t keep any record of the certificates it issues (approved CSRs are cleaned up about an hour after issue). This is done by watching CSR objects. When a client certificate has been signed and added to the CSR, certrevoker picks it up and creates a new object in Kubernetes called an IssuedCertificate which contains information about the cert including the credential ID. Not every certificate goes via the CSR API though (for example the ones kubeadm creates for kubeconfig files), so certrevoker also records any credential IDs it sees being used, which helps fill in the gaps. Then we have an authorization webhook for the cluster, which is placed in the authorization chain before the Node and RBAC authorizers. The API server is configured to call the webhook for any request authenticated with a client certificate, and part of the information passed to the webhook is the credential ID. The webhook checks that against the list of revoked certificates and, if the certificate has been revoked, returns an explicit deny. An explicit deny stops the authorization chain, so RBAC never gets a chance to allow the request. For anything that isn’t revoked the webhook returns “no opinion” and the request carries on to RBAC as normal. The API server caches these decisions briefly, so a revocation does take a few seconds to kick in. To revoke certificates there’s a web portal that is available to administrators. They log in with a Kubernetes token, and the portal uses that token for all its actions, so access is controlled by standard RBAC and the API server audit log shows who did what. From there they can view a list of certificates and pick one to revoke, along with a reason for the revocation. Revocations can also be undone, and if you’ve got a certificate or kubeconfig file that isn’t in the list, you can paste it into the portal to get its credential ID. As revocations are just Kubernetes objects, you can also manage them with kubectl if you prefer. Limitations As with any hack, there are some important caveats: system:masters certificates can’t be revoked. The API server allows any request from a member of the system:masters group before it calls any of the configured authorizers, so those requests never reach the webhook. Unfortunately that includes things like the kubeadm admin.conf certificate, which is one of the ones you’d most like to be able to revoke! It fails open. If certrevoker is unavailable, the API server treats that as “no opinion” and carries on to RBAC, so revoked certificates will work again until it comes back. This is deliberate, as in a kubeadm cluster the kubelets, controller manager and scheduler all authenticate using client certificates, so failing closed would break the cluster during an outage. The Future Whilst this is a useful option if you want to use certificate authentication in Kubernetes now, it’s obviously not the best solution long term. Here KEP 6285 will hopefully move forward providing a supported mechanism for rejecting specific client certificates.

This isn’t something stored in the certificate itself, it’s calculated by the API server as a SHA-256 hash of the certificate (X509SHA256=), which means that every client certificate can be uniquely identified, even ones that were issued long before v1.32. This opens up the idea that if we can intercept authorization decisions in the API server, we can have a mechanism to revoke access by marking a specific credential ID as revoked.

As a proof of concept I knocked up a tool called certrevoker which works as an operator in a Kubernetes cluster. This is very much a proof of concept, so don’t deploy it in a production cluster without a lot of improvement :D

The first stage is to keep track of the client certificates that exist in the cluster, as Kubernetes doesn’t keep any record of the certificates it issues (approved CSRs are cleaned up about an hour after issue). This is done by watching CSR objects. When a client certificate has been signed and added to the CSR, certrevoker picks it up and creates a new object in Kubernetes called an IssuedCertificate which contains information about the cert including the credential ID. Not every certificate goes via the CSR API though (for example the ones kubeadm creates for kubeconfig files), so certrevoker also records any credential IDs it sees being used, which helps fill in the gaps.

Then we have an authorization webhook for the cluster, which is placed in the authorization chain before the Node and RBAC authorizers. The API server is configured to call the webhook for any request authenticated with a client certificate, and part of the information passed to the webhook is the credential ID. The webhook checks that against the list of revoked certificates and, if the certificate has been revoked, returns an explicit deny. An explicit deny stops the authorization chain, so RBAC never gets a chance to allow the request. For anything that isn’t revoked the webhook returns “no opinion” and the request carries on to RBAC as normal. The API server caches these decisions briefly, so a revocation does take a few seconds to kick in.

To revoke certificates there’s a web portal that is available to administrators. They log in with a Kubernetes token, and the portal uses that token for all its actions, so access is controlled by standard RBAC and the API server audit log shows who did what. From there they can view a list of certificates and pick one to revoke, along with a reason for the revocation. Revocations can also be undone, and if you’ve got a certificate or kubeconfig file that isn’t in the list, you can paste it into the portal to get its credential ID. As revocations are just Kubernetes objects, you can also manage them with kubectl if you prefer.

Limitations

As with any hack, there are some important caveats:

  • system:masters certificates can’t be revoked. The API server allows any request from a member of the system:masters group before it calls any of the configured authorizers, so those requests never reach the webhook. Unfortunately that includes things like the kubeadm admin.conf certificate, which is one of the ones you’d most like to be able to revoke!

This is deliberate, as in a kubeadm cluster the kubelets, controller manager and scheduler all authenticate using client certificates, so failing closed would break the cluster during an outage.
The Future

Whilst this is a useful option if you want to use certificate authentication in Kubernetes now, it’s obviously not the best solution long term. Here KEP 6285 will hopefully move forward providing a supported mechanism for rejecting specific client certificates.

items.title: Detection engineering is hard, help your AI
items.summary: Many of us use AI in some form or another every day in our jobs. As someone who works in cybersecurity, I’m no different. When people talk about AI in the context of a SOC, many think about writing threat reports from online sources or closing alerts with a lot of tokens. But I think one discipline in security is still far from solved by AI: detection engineering. If you let any AI out there create a KQL detection they come up with the correct table names, in many cases even the columns, but often it ends when they hallucinate ActionTypes or completely miss how the XML is stored inside of one of the columns. And this is where a generated detection that looks good and runs well but never could detect anything can be more than harmful, it can lead to a false sense of protection and to missing alerts.
